# Results — Study 937 (Tranches) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One rule, twenty-one
schedules. The sleeve: on its rebalance day, hold **SPY** for the next month if SPY closed
above its **200-day** simple moving average, else hold **IEF**. "Monthly" means a 21-day
cycle, so there are 21 distinct rebalance offsets — 21 books running the identical rule.
Lag, in the house form: the state read from closes through day t is the position that earns
the return of t+1 — **one** `shift`, so execution sits at the **t close**, not a day later
(a second day of delay is re-run below and changes nothing). Cost is **one-way bps x traded
notional / NAV**, where a switch trades 2 x |Δ position| (sell one leg, buy the other), so a
full switch pays 2 x the one-way rate; nothing is shorted, so there is **no borrow leg**.
Tranching: split the capital into N sleeves rebalanced on N offsets spread round the cycle,
each compounding on its own (overlapping portfolios); the book is their NAV-weighted
average. Sharpes are **excess-of-cash**. Daily **total-return** closes (`yfinance`,
`auto_adjust=True`). As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY, IEF (the sleeve legs) | 2002-07-30 → 2026-06-30 | 6,018 | Fingerprint `e8f9552be0ac` |
| the 21 books, after the 200-day warm-up | 2003-06-16 → 2026-06-30 | 5,797 | — |

Cash leg: **^IRX** (13-week bill discount yield) accrued daily — a **PROXY**, since ^IRX is
a quote, not a fund. The tradable **BIL** total return is carried as a cross-check on its
own 2007+ window and moves the answer by 0.008 of a Sharpe point. The sleeve is in SPY
**81.0%** of days.

## The cone — the same rule, 21 different rebalance dates

Each row is the distribution of outcomes across the 21 possible placements of an N-tranche
book. "Terminal spread" is how much richer the luckiest placement finished than the
unluckiest over the 23 years.

| N tranches | Excess Sharpe (mean) | sd | min | max | range | CAGR sd | Terminal spread | Traded/yr (both legs) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **1** (one date) | +0.631 | **0.066** | +0.499 | +0.755 | **0.256** | 0.86 pp | **95.1%** | 2.74x |
| **4** | +0.670 | 0.023 | +0.634 | +0.726 | 0.092 | 0.29 pp | 27.3% | 2.71x |
| **12** | +0.675 | 0.010 | +0.662 | +0.696 | 0.034 | 0.10 pp | 7.7% | 2.70x |
| **21** (every date) | +0.676 | **0.000** | +0.676 | +0.676 | **0.000** | 0.00 pp | **0.0%** | 2.70x |

- The **cone is large**: an arbitrary calendar choice moves the reported Sharpe of an
  identical rule by up to **0.256** and the 23-year terminal wealth by **95%**.
- The **fix works, and works fast**: sd(N)/sd(1) = **1.000 / 0.340 / 0.152 / 0.000** against
  the naive 1/√N reference **1.000 / 0.500 / 0.289 / 0.218** — four tranches already remove
  two-thirds of the dispersion, and the full 21 remove it *exactly* (every rotation is the
  same set of offsets, so there is nothing left to be lucky about).
- The **fix is free in turnover**: 2.741x NAV/yr on one date → **2.700x** tranched
  (**−1.5%**). Each tranche trades 1/N of NAV, so the notional does not multiply. (That
  figure counts **both legs** of every switch, i.e. ≈1.37x one-way.)

## What tranching actually buys

| | one date (mean of 21) | 21 tranches | change |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Excess Sharpe | +0.631 | **+0.676** | **+0.044** |
| CAGR | 9.63% | 9.70% | **+0.07 pp/yr** |
| Vol | 13.30% | 12.32% | −0.98 pp |
| Max drawdown (mean / worst placement) | −31.0% / −35.4% | −26.2% | +4.8 pp |

The Sharpe gain is **almost entirely variance, not return**: seven basis points a year of
CAGR against a full point of volatility. Tranching is not an alpha source — the tranched
book *is* the average of the 21 dates, so its mean return cannot be anything else. What it
removes is the dispersion around that average.

## Block bootstrap (1,000 draws, 21-day blocks, resampled jointly across the 21 books)

| Statistic | Point | 95% interval | share < 0 | what the interval is worth |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| Cone sd at N = 1 | 0.066 | [0.054, 0.145] | — | a **spread band, not a test** |
| Tranching Sharpe gain | +0.044 | [+0.014, +0.073] | 0.3% | a real interval (≈ \|*t*\| 2.7) |

**Read the first row with care — it is not evidence of anything.** A standard deviation
cannot be negative, so "the CI excludes zero" is true by construction for *any* set of 21
non-identical books and proves nothing about the cone. The band is also strongly
right-skewed, with the point estimate sitting almost on its lower edge (0.066 vs a 2.5th
percentile of 0.054): resampling blocks of days scrambles the calendar phases that generate
the cone, so the bootstrap sees *more* dispersion than the tape does. Treat it as a
sampling band on a descriptive quantity.

The **gain** row is the study's only interval that could have come out negative and did
not: 0.3% of 1,000 draws below zero, the Gaussian equivalent of |*t*| ≈ 2.7 (not 2.9 —
Φ⁻¹(0.997) = 2.75). Even that is a near-mechanical quantity: averaging imperfectly
correlated books at a fixed mean return almost has to shrink the vol. The honest reading is
that the numbers confirm arithmetic, not that they discover a premium.

## Is the lucky date forecastable?

- Ex-post **best offset 2** (+0.755) vs **worst offset 17** (+0.499): gap 0.256, HAC *t* on
  the daily return difference **+1.98** — and that *t* is **selection-biased by
  construction** (argmax against argmin of 21 correlated books). It is an upper bound on
  how impressive the cone can be made to look, not evidence of skill.
- **Persistence** (split 2014-12-17): the two halves' offset rankings correlate
  **ρ = +0.309**. The first-half winner (offset 2) ranked **2/21** in the second half, worth
  **+0.620** against the 21-date average **+0.562** — i.e. **+0.058**. Compared
  **same-window**, tranching was worth **+0.042** over those same rows (+0.044 in the first
  half), so *chasing the ex-post winner actually beat the free fix by +0.016 in that one
  out-of-sample half*. That is one draw, not a finding: the date was selected by looking at
  the first half, the actual second-half winner was a different offset (9), the rank
  transfer is only ρ = +0.309, and a chased date puts the whole book back into the lottery
  it just won. We report it against us rather than round it the convenient way.
- The two rules' offset rankings correlate **ρ = +0.556**, so part of the cone is probably
  a shared calendar/flow footprint rather than pure noise (cf. study 604). We are not
  claiming it is unforecastable — only that the forecast we can build from half a sample is
  one draw wide, while the tranching fix needs no forecast at all.
- **An edge-free rule has a wider cone — across seeds, not just the one we drew.** An
  exposure-matched **random-timing** rule on the same legs disperses **sd 0.103, range
  0.462, terminal spread 419%** on seed 937, and tranches to a single point too. One random
  schedule is itself a lottery ticket, so we swept **20 seeds**: cone sd **mean 0.093,
  median 0.094, min 0.065, max 0.121**, wider than the trend rule's 0.066 in **19 of 20**.
  The quoted 0.103 is an upper-half draw; the distribution is the claim. Timing luck is an
  artefact of the *schedule*, not a symptom of edge.

## Robustness

**Two eras (split 2014-01-01).** The cone and the fix are in both halves:

| Era | n | Sharpe (one date) | sd | range | Tranched | Gain | Traded/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2003–2013 | 2,656 | +0.717 | 0.096 | 0.341 | +0.762 | **+0.045** | 2.82x → 2.78x |
| 2014–2026 | 3,119 | +0.604 | 0.056 | 0.218 | +0.645 | **+0.041** | 2.69x → 2.67x |

**Cost sweep** (one-way bps on traded notional; no shorts, so no borrow):

| One-way cost | one date (sd) | 21 tranches | Gain |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.642 (0.065) | +0.687 | +0.045 |
| 1 bp | +0.640 (0.066) | +0.684 | +0.045 |
| 5 bps | +0.631 (0.066) | +0.676 | +0.044 |
| 10 bps | +0.621 (0.068) | +0.665 | +0.044 |
| 25 bps | +0.590 (0.071) | +0.632 | +0.042 |

Friction is not what drives this: the gain is flat from 0 to 25 bps, and the cone actually
*widens* slightly with cost (0.065 → 0.071), because the unlucky dates trade more.

**Broker tickets — an ASSUMPTION sweep, not a tape measurement.** Proportional cost is
flat in N, but tickets are not: N tranches means N separate pairs of orders on a switch.

| N | tickets/yr | drag at 0.5 bp/ticket | drag at 2 bp/ticket |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 2.6 | 0.013%/yr | 0.052%/yr |
| 4 | 11.0 | 0.055%/yr | 0.219%/yr |
| 12 | 32.3 | 0.162%/yr | 0.647%/yr |
| 21 | 57.6 | **0.288%/yr** | **1.151%/yr** |

A ticket costs a fixed sum, so its bps-of-NAV depend entirely on account size: at
institutional size the drag rounds to zero, at retail size the 21-tranche book can pay more
in tickets (0.29%/yr) than the +0.07 pp/yr of CAGR it adds. **Tax is not modelled** and
runs the same way — N tranches create N times the realisation events.

**One more day of execution delay.** The books above trade at the close that formed the
signal. Assume instead that you only get filled at the *next* close (`state.shift(1)`, a
second lag): single-date Sharpe **+0.622** (sd **0.071**, range 0.270) → tranched **+0.666**,
gain **+0.044**. The cone and the fix are not artefacts of the execution assumption.

**Cross-checks.**

- **12-1 momentum sleeve** (hold whichever of SPY/IEF has the better 12-month-minus-last-month
  return): the same shape on a different rule — cone sd **0.039**, range 0.165, terminal
  spread **77.7%**, collapsing to 0.000 at 21 tranches; gain **+0.013**, turnover 2.81x →
  2.82x.
- **Tradable BIL cash leg** (2007-05-30 → 2026-06-30, n = 4,581): cone sd **0.051**, range
  0.206, gain **+0.046**. The ^IRX proxy on the same window gives +0.674 against BIL's
  +0.682 — a 0.008 Sharpe difference, so the proxy is not carrying the result.
- **Synthetic control** (machinery proof only, never supports the stamp; 6 seeds, 40 years
  each). Planted regime: the sleeve beats an exposure-matched random control by **+0.450**
  (min +0.249) — the detector fires. Flat null: **−0.003** (min −0.188, max +0.175) — it
  stays quiet. In **both** worlds the cone is there (sd 0.048 and 0.053) and tranching kills
  it exactly (0.000), with a small positive gain (+0.024 / +0.005). The fix is schedule
  arithmetic; it does not need the rule to have edge, and it does not manufacture any.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Real.** Rebalance timing luck is not a synthetic curiosity: on the real
  SPY/IEF tape the same monthly rule prints Sharpes from **+0.499 to +0.755** and terminal
  wealth **95.1%** apart depending only on which day of the month you happen to rebalance.
  *There is no null hypothesis to reject here, and we do not pretend otherwise* — dispersion
  across schedules is a **measurement**, not a premium, and no interval on a standard
  deviation can testify for it. What earns the stamp is that the measurement is large on
  the real tape and reproduces on every cut we tried: both eras (0.096 / 0.056), a second
  rule (0.039), the tradable cash leg (0.051), a second day of execution delay (0.071), and
  an edge-free random rule that is *wider* in 19 of 20 seeds (mean 0.093). Tranching removes
  it: **exactly** zero at 21 tranches, two-thirds gone at four, at **−1.5%** turnover, for a
  Sharpe gain of **+0.044** — the one interval here that could have been negative and was
  not ([+0.014, +0.073], 0.3% of draws, |*t*| ≈ 2.7), and even that is close to arithmetic.
  What we are *not* claiming: no single rebalance date is significantly better than another
  (the ex-post best-minus-worst HAC *t* is **+1.98**, below 2, and selection-biased on top).
  Survivorship: SPY and IEF are surviving mega-ETFs picked with hindsight, but the cone is
  measured *across dates on the identical assets*, so survivorship cannot create it.
- **Tradability — Fragile.** What is bankable is thin and conditional. The gain is
  variance, not return (**+0.07 pp/yr** of CAGR), and the one cost that scales with N is the
  one we cannot read off the tape: at 0.5 bp of NAV per ticket the 21-tranche book pays
  **0.29%/yr** — four times the CAGR it adds — while the same book inside a large fund pays
  nothing. Taxes push the same way. The honest operating point is **four tranches**: 66% of
  the cone gone for 11 tickets a year, and every one of the 21 four-tranche rotations
  (+0.634 to +0.726) beat the average single date (+0.631). Tranch to stop your track record
  being an accident of the calendar, not to make money.
